reports.title: Angler Borrows Friend’s Lure, Immediately Catches Record Smallmouth
reports.text:
When Austin Schiefer borrowed a bait from his buddy as they fished Green Bay in Wisconsin, he had no idea the results would be so dramatic.
Ted Johnson, his longtime fishing partner, had been using a Japanese-made soft plastic jerkbait to catch big smallmouth bass they spotted on Livescope, an electronics unit that shows real-time movement of fish.
Schiefer, who runs a company that makes soft-plastic baits, had left his homemade minnow imitations at home. So, after some good-natured ribbing, Johnson suggested that Schiefer go to a lighter-action rod and use one of his high-priced baits.
On his first cast with the bait, Schiefer caught the biggest smallmouth bass ever reported in Wisconsin —…

reports.title: What Lures We’re Throwing in November 2026
reports.text:
Fall is finally in full swing. The air temps are plummeting, the leaves are rusting their way to a new hue, and the bass are biting. Baitfish migrations are always super important in the fall, as massive schools of shad and other forage make their way from deep to shallow. With baitfish abundant, the bass have a keen eye, and using baits that “match the hatch” become a big deal in the fall. With this in mind, here are some of the lures I’ll be throwing around the Southeast this month, as well as November favorites from Bassmaster Elite and MLF Bass Pro Tour Angler of the Year champions, Trey McKinney and Zack Birge.

reports.title: Thankfulness: so much to be thankful for
reports.text:
Cooler temperatures are just one reason to be thankful
N ovember is a month I’m thankful to see roll around every year. The cooler temperatures and frosty mornings are a reprieve from the intense heat domes we’ve suffered through these past summers. July and August triple-digit readings have forced me to sweat profusely instead of lightly perspiring. It’s wonderful to stand in cold water, chilled, and try to catch a trout on a fly. Exhaling slowly, I watch my damp breath turn into ice crystals and disappear. What a beautiful morning to be here. Quiet, alone, and time to ponder the things I’ve been too busy to think about otherwise.
Wading a cold mountain stream in November is almost a…

reports.title: Why The One That Got Away Can Be So Memorable
reports.text:
Anglers Journal founding editor Bill Sisson mentions the term ‘nursing home fish’ in his book “ Seasons of the Striper: Pursuing the Great American Gamefish .” It refers to fish caught long ago, the memories of which keep you company even when you’re too old to wet a line. These are the fish you can still see when you close your eyes, still feel their heft when you dream.
But I think that the ones that got away are just as important. Ask any angler about their most memorable fishing trip and sooner or later, you’ll hear about a fish that they couldn’t land.

reports.title: CN How To Nov 2026 How To: Crappie Dan explains how shadows, current, and underwater structure influence crappie behavior.
reports.text:
How To: Crappie Dan explains how shadows, current, and underwater structure influence crappie behavior.
In this episode of The Playbook, Crappie Dan explains how shadows, current, and underwater structure influence crappie and bass behavior. Fish often face into the current, positioning themselves where baitfish will naturally approach. During sunny conditions, they tend to hold in the shade created by stumps, brush, overhanging trees, and shoreline drop-offs, often near the edge of the light.
The key to success is proper boat positioning and bait placement. When casting or jigging, position your bait up current so it moves naturally toward the fish. Approaching from behind can spook them…

reports.text:
Berkley Powerbait Drip Minnow 3″
Realism of plastic minnows just took a giant leap forward. The Berkley Powerbait Drip Minnow features high-definition true colors, molded scale patterns, glitter flecks that mimic real fish, realistic eyes and even internal guts that are visible on translucent color patterns. If these minnows looked any more real, they’d start gasping for air and moving their gills. The bait’s body tapers to a “drip” shaped tail that doesn’t require much speed to get a good thumping movement and moves easily when twitched or shaken. MSRP $11 for a pack of 6.

Crappie Basics: Finding and Catching Crappie in Cold Weather

November can be one of the most productive months for crappie fishing. reports.title: Bank-Fishing Teen Nearly Breaks 21-Year-Old State Largemouth Bass Record
reports.text:
Some time around mid-morning on Oct. 3, 14-year-old Luke Mulholland of Zumbrota, Minnesota, took a break from his usual trout fishing. He decided to try for bass at Cascade Lake, located near Rochester.
He was casting a half-foot long Bucca Baits Trick Shad swim bait when he saw a disturbance on the lake surface.
“I was fishing and I saw a wake in the water, and I cast at it and I thought I snagged a log, it was just heavy,” said Luke, who’s been fishing since age 3.
A Largemouth That Felt Like a Log
But when the log started moving and hard fought his tackle, he knew it wasn’t a snag. It was so heavy, he then thought he hooked a turtle.

reports.title: Hit Lake Murray’s brush for fall crappie
reports.text:
Don’t miss the fall crappie bite
A s Lake Murray’s water temperature cools down in October, Capt. Brad Taylor of Taylor Outdoors said the crappie fishing gets cranked up.
“October is a great month because you can catch crappie in a number of ways, really just about any way you want to catch them will work,” he said.
One way Taylor targets them this time of year is by fishing brush in the main river channel.
“Fall is kind of a magical time of year for Lake Murray because the shad start working up the river,” he said. “And the crappie follow the bait. If you can find the bait, which isn’t too difficult using electronics, then you can find the crappie.”

Paddlin’ with Madalyn: Stay Safe, Be Seen
by Madalyn Roberts
Before taking a kayak out on the water, be sure to familiarize yourself with the light requirements for your setup. From sunset to sunrise—and during other times of restricted visibility such as rain or heavy fog—kayaks that are paddled by hand or pedal-powered require some type of flashing white light. Motorized kayaks require both a continuously visible, 360-degree white light pole on the stern and standard navigation lights on the bow, red on port (left) and green on starboard (right).

reports.title: Crappie Basics: Match the Hatch for More Crappie
reports.text:
Matching your jig to the size and shape of the main crappie forage can greatly increase your number of hookups.
Crappie Basics: Match the Hatch for More Crappie
By Keith Sutton
One of the simplest ways to improve your crappie fishing is to give the fish what they’re already looking for. That means matching your jig to the size and general shape of the forage crappie are feeding on.
If 2-inch minnows make up a big part of the crappie diet in the lake you’re fishing, for example, a 2-inch jig is a logical choice. If the fish are eating tiny shiners, you’ll probably do better with a smaller offering. The same principle applies when shad, fathead minnows or other forage dominate the menu.
